questions.q: What is Chubukov's very first reaction when Lomov announces he has come to ask for Natalya's hand in marriage?
questions.a: Chubukov is overjoyed, embraces and kisses Lomov, calls him "my angel" and "my treasure," and says he has always hoped for this match. A wrong answer (e.g., "He is suspicious" or "He asks about Lomov's health") reveals the student has not noticed the performative warmth that masks his transactional mindset — a key Board exam trap where students confuse surface politeness with genuine emotion.

questions.q: Why does Chubukov suddenly turn hostile during the argument over Oxen Meadows, even though he welcomed Lomov warmly minutes earlier?
questions.a: Chubukov's hostility reveals his true priority: property rights outweigh the marriage alliance. When Lomov claims the Meadows, Chubukov sees a threat to his estate, not a son-in-law. He abandons the "fatherly" role to defend his land. A wrong answer (e.g., "He loses his temper because Lomov is rude") misses the satirical point — Chekhov shows how quickly social masks drop when material interests are challenged. This is a classic Board exam misconception: confusing character inconsistency with deliberate authorial satire.

questions.q: In the second argument (about dogs), Chubukov says: "I don't want your dog... I'm not going to give my daughter to a man who doesn't know a good dog." Apply the concept of *dramatic irony* to explain what the audience understands that Chubukov does not.
questions.a: The audience knows the proposal is the *real* purpose of Lomov's visit, but Chubukov treats the dog argument as a legitimate reason to cancel the marriage. The irony: Chubukov claims to reject Lomov over a dog, yet moments later he forces the engagement because the economic match is too advantageous. Steps: (1) Identify the stated reason (dog superiority); (2) Identify the real reason (property alliance); (3) Note the audience sees the contradiction; (4) Conclude Chubukov is performing outrage to gain leverage. A wrong answer that only describes the dog quarrel misses the irony — a Board exam requirement for "analysis of dramatic technique."

questions.q: Compare Chubukov's behaviour in the first half of the play (before Lomov faints) with his behaviour after Lomov revives. What does this shift reveal about his view of marriage?
questions.a: Before the faint: Chubukov threatens to throw Lomov out, calls him "a malicious, double-faced intriguer," and tells Natalya "don't dare" to marry him. After the faint: He instantly blesses them, shoves Lomov's hand into Natalya's, and orders champagne. The shift proves marriage is a *business deal* he cannot afford to lose — Lomov's inheritance (300 roubles annual income) secures Natalya's future. A weak answer listing only the insults vs. the blessing without the *economic motive* fails the Board's "character analysis with textual evidence" rubric.

questions.q: Evaluate the statement: "Chubukov is a loving father who ultimately wants his daughter's happiness." Use two specific pieces of evidence from the play to support or refute.
questions.a: Refute. Evidence 1: He uses Natalya as bait — "She's willing... she's in love" — to manipulate Lomov into accepting the Meadows compromise. Evidence 2: When Lomov revives, Chubukov ignores Natalya's feelings ("I'll give her away... I don't care") and forces the union to secure the alliance. A "support" answer using only his initial "my angel" dialogue shows the student cannot distinguish performative affection from genuine care — a frequent Board exam error in character evaluation questions.

questions.q: Write a 4-line monologue from Chubukov's perspective *after* the curtain falls, revealing his true thoughts about the marriage he just arranged.
questions.a: *Sample criteria for a strong answer:* (1) References the 300 roubles/land deal; (2) Shows cynicism about love; (3) Uses Chubukov's voice (blunt, possessive); (4) Connects to the play's satire. Example: *"She's married, the land is signed, the dog is forgotten — / Three hundred roubles yearly, nicely begotten. / Love? Ha! A word for fools and poets' rhyme — / I've sold my daughter for a very good time."* A poor answer expressing genuine joy or fatherly pride misses the satirical lens entirely.

questions.q: Fill in the blank: Ivan Chubukov is a wealthy ______ and father of Natalya in Anton Chekhov's one-act farce *The Proposal*.
Fill in the blank: Imagine you are at a family wedding where the uncle ______ starts shouting about a boundary wall instead of blessing the couple.
What is Ivan Chubukov? State the definition given in this lesson.
questions.a: Ivan Chubukov is a wealthy landowner and father of Natalya in Anton Chekhov's one-act farce *The Proposal*.

questions.q: What common mix-up does this lesson flag about Ivan Chubukov?
questions.a: Students often treat Chubukov's mood swings as "inconsistent writing" or "bad temper" rather than *deliberate satirical characterisation*.

questions.q: What must you be able to do to master this topic?
questions.a: The student must be able to: (1) Trace Chubukov's shifting attitudes across the three stages of the proposal (initial welcome, argument over Oxen Meadows/dogs, final forced blessing) using textual evidence; (2) Explain how his behaviour satirises the reduction of marriage to a property transaction in 19th-century Russian landed gentry.
